paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, dated 1990, which came to the shop with no record of the garden it was picked from. That was common for its era. Buyers began choosing by [named mountains and villages](sheng:history-modern) rather than factory brands only after the collectors’ boom of the 1980s and 1990s.

Raw pu’er is never pushed through [a rapid fermentation](sheng:aging). Its leaf is [dried in the sun](sheng:making) rather than with hot air, so some of the leaf’s own activity survives, and the tea keeps changing on its own for years. At thirty-six years, this cake is well past the twenty that many in the trade wait for before they call a [raw pu’er aged](sheng:ageing). Heat and humidity decide how fast that change happens, so the way it was [stored](sheng:storage) is part of its history.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
